title: AI auditing: Organisational evidence must remain auditable
desc: Centers lifecycle records, social impact and remediation while treating independence and evidence integrity as unresolved assurance risks.

kps.k: Both papers locate AI accountability in auditable organizational conduct, not model performance alone.
kps.d: Raji and colleagues’ Closing the AI Accountability Gap proposes lifecycle auditing to translate declared ethical principles into development controls. AI Governance and the Verification Gap adds a claimed formal justification: limits on comprehensive model assurance create evidentiary problems for liability, oversight and redress. The papers differ in emphasis—ethical governance versus legally enforceable assurance—rather than directly disagreeing. Neither presents process governance as a substitute for technical testing or broader accountability.

qs.q: The contribution of this paper is not the invention of process-based governance, but the provision of a new and more robust formal justification for why, in the face of computational intractability, it represents a rational and necessary path forward.
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Relying solely on process governance without any technical inspection of the model is insufficient, while relying solely on technical inspection is impossible.
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

kps.k: The limits of complete assurance do not establish that practical safety testing is futile.
kps.d: AI Governance and the Verification Gap accepts that heuristic audits, behavioral testing and sound engineering can provide reasonable safety for most systems. Its stronger concern targets catastrophic risks and widely deployed systems where rare failures accumulate. It cites trigger-dependent malicious behavior and limitations in circuit discovery, then argues that tests cannot exclude unknown mechanisms or prevent gaming. Whether heuristics meet a legally sufficient safety standard for high-stakes systems remains unresolved; the cited research does not itself settle that legal question.

qs.q: For the vast majority of AI systems, a robust portfolio of heuristic auditing, behavioral testing, and sound engineering practice can provide a sufficient and reasonable standard of safety.
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

qs.q: It applies primarily to those high-stakes systems where the potential for catastrophic or systemic harm necessitates a higher standard of assurance, and to widely deployed systems where even low-probability failures can create substantial integrated harm at scale.
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Lifecycle records should connect risk assessment to decisions, remediation and continuing oversight.
kps.d: Closing the AI Accountability Gap organizes SMACTR around Scoping, Mapping, Artifact Collection, Testing and Reflection. Interviews, model cards, datasheets and design histories should reconstruct assumptions and decisions, inform mitigation and support abandoning projects whose risks outweigh benefits. AI Governance and the Verification Gap extends the evidentiary approach through signed commits, peer reviews, testing logs and communications, with cross-checks against personnel accounts. Both recognize that changing models, deployment contexts and incomplete documentation complicate audits; the latter proposes adaptive metrics and risk-triggered re-audits.

qs.q: This evidentiary trail includes version control systems with cryptographically signed and timestamped commits, records of peer code reviews, project management tickets detailing bug fixes and feature development, logs from automated testing and deployment pipelines, and internal communications [127].
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Audit standards must address social impact, not simply technical reliability or checklist compliance.
kps.d: Closing the AI Accountability Gap cites an external facial-analysis audit’s demographic disparities to argue for documenting social context and power dynamics. It treats metric choices as value judgments and recommends diverse ethical review. The authors acknowledge that organizational AI principles can be vague but use them as provisional standards where universal ones are absent. AI Governance and the Verification Gap emphasizes adaptive lifecycle metrics and affected-user feedback. Together, these proposals leave a substantive governance task: deciding what harms and objectives an audit should assess, rather than assuming documentation alone establishes acceptability.

qs.q: An effective governance system would establish a meta-process guided by frameworks like the NIST AI RMF's Measure and Manage functions for continuously evaluating which metrics are most salient for a given application and risk context [56].
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Internal access improves auditability, but independence and evidence integrity remain unresolved risks.
kps.d: Closing the AI Accountability Gap argues that internal auditors can inspect processes unavailable to outsiders and intervene earlier, while acknowledging external auditors’ relative insulation from organizational pressure. It therefore treats internal and external scrutiny as complementary. AI Governance and the Verification Gap adds that valuable certifications and safe harbors can encourage fraudulent compliance. Secure logging, interviews, whistleblower channels and penalties aim to make deception harder and costlier, not impossible. Certification would signal process integrity, not guarantee model safety.

kps.k: The legal-policy proposal would exchange liability benefits for substantive transparency.
kps.d: AI Governance and the Verification Gap proposes risk-tiered liability, including strict liability for designated high-risk applications, research protections and safe harbors earned through deep regulatory transparency. It recommends mandatory NIST AI RMF implementation for federal agencies and contractors and explores FTC Act Section 5 as a route against unsupported safety claims. These are policy recommendations and proposed legal applications, not descriptions of an established liability regime. For enterprise buyers, the practical implication is to demand auditable vendor processes and data-provenance evidence rather than rely on developer attestations alone.

qs.q: It creates powerful economic and legal incentives that make superficial compliance a high-risk business strategy by establishing distinct, risk-appropriate liability defaults and safe harbors for non-commercial, general commercial, and high-risk applications.
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Its central feature is an administrative pathway that allows developers to earn a more predictable and less demanding legal standard in exchange for deep transparency with an expert regulator, providing legal certainty for industry and promoting the adoption of auditable safety processes.
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

kps.k: The cluster offers governance frameworks, not demonstrated evidence that those frameworks reduce AI harm.
kps.d: Closing the AI Accountability Gap draws on auditing precedents from other industries and fictional applications, not measured SMACTR deployment outcomes; it leaves the selection of systems for audit outside its scope. AI Governance and the Verification Gap combines cited technical research, surveys and legal reasoning, while acknowledging implementation difficulties. Its reported 2025 global survey—58% regular workplace AI use versus 34% reporting organizational guidance—motivates oversight concerns but does not demonstrate audit effectiveness. Both papers support practical experimentation with governance while preserving uncertainty about effectiveness, transferability and residual risk.

qs.q: A 2025 global survey illustrates this divide, finding that while 58% of employees regularly use AI tools for work, only 34% report that their organization has a policy or even guidance on the use of these systems [5].
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources accept the principal proposition that AI accountability requires auditable organizational evidence across the lifecycle, rather than reliance on model-performance testing alone. They materially develop it by specifying what auditability entails: documented development decisions, risk assessment, testing, remediation, deployment review, continuing monitoring, and artifacts accessible to external scrutiny. Their common rationale is that technical assurance is incomplete and context-dependent, while organizational processes can create a tractable evidentiary basis for intervention and accountability. Material variation lies in emphasis. Closing the AI Accountability Gap foregrounds ethical governance, social context and the SMACTR internal-audit workflow, with internal and external auditing treated as complementary. AI Governance and the Verification Gap supplies a legal and technical justification based on persistent verification limits, then extends the approach through tamper-resistant records, cross-validation, risk-tiered liability, regulatory transparency and sanctions for fraudulent compliance. Both retain important qualifications: process audits must complement technical testing; independence, evidence integrity and audit selection remain unresolved; and the proposed frameworks are not demonstrated evidence that auditing reduces harm. This assessment characterizes only the curated sources supplied, not academia or researchers generally.

qs.q: The contribution of this paper is not the invention of process-based governance, but the provision of a new and more robust formal justification for why, in the face of computational intractability, it represents a rational and necessary path forward.
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The 2020 source accepts the proposition that AI accountability depends on auditable organizational evidence and materially develops it through SMACTR, an end-to-end internal auditing framework spanning development, documentation, ethical assessment, remediation and deployment decisions. Its central reason is that technical reliability alone cannot establish ethical acceptability: organizations must preserve records of assumptions, decisions, social context and risk responses so conduct can be examined. It also strengthens the proposition by making internal and external assurance complementary—internal auditors have earlier and deeper access, while transparent artifacts enable independent scrutiny. Material qualifications remain: internal auditors may face organizational pressure; rapid iteration, incomplete documentation and variable deployment contexts impede auditability; audit selection lies outside the framework; and the paper offers cross-industry precedents and hypothetical applications rather than measured evidence that SMACTR reduces harm. These limitations qualify the proposed mechanism but do not displace its support for lifecycle auditability.

The 2025 source accepts the proposition that AI accountability requires auditable organisational evidence rather than reliance on model-performance testing alone, and materially develops it for adoption at scale. Its principal reason is that widespread deployment magnifies the consequences of persistent limits on comprehensive technical assurance: rare failures may accumulate, opaque foundation-model dependencies create supply-chain risks, and model evolution can render static assessments obsolete. It therefore specifies an auditable evidentiary architecture—signed and timestamped commits, peer reviews, project tickets, testing and deployment logs, and internal communications—supplemented by secure logging, personnel interviews, whistleblower channels, risk-triggered re-audits and penalties for fraudulent compliance. It also extends the proposition into policy through risk-tiered liability and legal benefits exchanged for deep regulatory transparency. Material qualifications prevent this from becoming an audit-only argument: the source says practical technical testing remains sufficient for many systems and necessary for all, while stronger process controls are especially important for high-stakes or widely deployed uses. It also treats certifications as signals of process integrity rather than guarantees of safety and acknowledges that process evidence can itself be manipulated. Thus, the source strengthens the cluster’s central proposition while preserving its concerns about residual assurance limits, evidence integrity and unproven governance effectiveness.

qs.q: The contribution of this paper is not the invention of process-based governance, but the provision of a new and more robust formal justification for why, in the face of computational intractability, it represents a rational and necessary path forward.
qs.a: AI Governance and the Verification Gap: A Framework for Law and Policy Under Computational Intractability · Academia · 2025
